verdict: OK to lend in Bharuch wagon/coach supply chain, but only to units with confirmed Indian Railways/private orders and a working-capital cycle under control; avoid pure wagon assemblers waiting on delayed tenders.
title: Bharuch railway wagons & coaches: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**A wagon or coach builder converts steel, castings, bearings and bought-out electricals into a finished vehicle against a specific Railway or metro order, and gets paid on dispatch and inspection, not on production.** Cash sits in raw steel and work-in-progress for months before the first cheque. The peer rating file shows exactly this: Oriental Rail's working capital cycle was 208 days in FY24, improved from 223 days in FY23, and still called elongated [10]. So when a proposal lands, check the inventory holding period and collection period separately; if the cycle is above 200 days, ask what the order-wise dispatch schedule is and who the inspecting agency is.

## Where value and cash sit now
**Pricing power is thin and input costs are moving faster than price revisions.** Timken India's Q2 FY27 call (30 Oct 2026) cites sharp increases in carbides, steel, gas and labour, says the industry cannot absorb them and must pass them on, with a timing gap; 130 bps of gross-margin pressure split roughly half to mix (lower rail) and half to input-cost/pricing timing [1]. Rail tenders were delayed, holding back the quarter's rail contribution [1]. So on any proposal, check the price-variation clause in the customer contract; if there is none, ask how much of the order book is fixed-price.

## The growth opportunity, and who to pursue
**The national output data is strong but the local picture is thin.** IIP for NIC 30 is +25.3% YoY and +22.7% Apr-to-date [D]. Gujarat GST collections are +11.9% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1% [D]. Bank credit to the segment is +27.0% YoY against output +22.7%, a gap of +4.3 pp [D] — money is moving in faster than output, which is where over-lending starts. Bharuch-specific rail news is only station infrastructure: a 12-metre foot overbridge under construction [2], and a demand for a Bharuch–Dahej rapid service [3]. Neither is wagon demand. **Pursue Tier-2 component and fabrication suppliers to the Bharuch plant ecosystem and coach-interior/metro sub-suppliers with confirmed orders; avoid standalone wagon assemblers whose order book depends on the next tender.** Titagarh's order book of ~5,300 wagons is entirely scheduled for FY27 delivery, with monthly run-rate scalable to 1,000 wagons once new tenders are awarded [5] — that is the demand signal to lend against, not hope.

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the order, not the balance sheet.** Take assignment of receivables or escrow of Railway/metro payments where the customer is a PSU; keep fund-based limits sized to the 208-day-type cycle [10], not to peak revenue. Take every month: order-book statement with delivery dates, dispatch and inspection certificates, age-wise inventory, and the top-five customer payment status. If the borrower's largest order is a private wagon buyer, ask for that buyer's payment history before sanction.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch the tender calendar and the input-price pass-through, not the topline.** Timken's Bharuch plant averaged roughly 60% utilisation in Q2, with CRB below 60% and SRB at 70% [1] — under-utilisation plus cost inflation is the pattern to fear. If a borrower's dispatch slips a month against the Railway schedule, ask for the revised inspection date; if two months, restructure to receivable-backed limits.
watch: Dispatch slips one month vs Railway schedule -> ask for revised inspection date; two months -> shift to receivable-backed limits
Cycle crosses 200 days [10] -> freeze fresh fund-based enhancement until it comes back
Fixed-price orders exceed half the book -> reprice or reduce exposure
No new wagon tender awarded for two quarters -> stop new wagon-only assembler proposals
